The record:
Write the overview of the executive synopsis for the incident on io-shop below: a short paragraph in plain words, for the people who lead the company rather than the engineers who responded - what happened, how long it lasted, what it cost the business and the people who responded, and how it was resolved.

What a reader saw: The slowest io-shop requests took far longer to load
Why, in plain words: Switching on a feature made the shop use a new way of working out a shopper's typical spend, and that method likely slows down sharply for shoppers with a long purchase history, so their pages took much longer to load.

Figures:
- How long it lasted: 7m 24s {duration}
- What it cost the shop in takings (estimated by Argus): none {customer_loss}
- Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one.

What was done to end it:
- Argus: reverted the feature flag typical-purchase-feature - confirmed, still in place
- Argus: proposed a fix, PR #545 - opened as a draft

Name {duration} and {customer_loss} in your overview.
Write no figure yourself - not in digits, not spelled out, and not as a word that sizes it ("a brief outage", "a minor loss", "tripled"). Where a figure goes, write its name, braces and all, and the synopsis writes the figure in.
Say nothing about how the incident was resolved beyond what the list of what was done says: a draft fix has not run, and nothing it would do has happened.
Speak of Argus by name, never as "we", "our" or "us": Argus is the system that responded, and each line of what was done says who did it.
Where you say who was affected, say which ones, as the cause does, or that some were, where it does not say which - never how many, and never all of them, where the cause does not say all.
Keep "likely" on what the cause says is likely, and only there.

Call submit_executive_overview with your overview.

The postmortem it is written from:
The slowest io-shop requests took far longer to load while typical-purchase-feature was on
Incident: HighLatency on io-shop
Date: Nov 11, 2026, 03:18 to 03:25:24 UTC
Status: Draft. 1 of 6 action items are done.
Written by: Argus Postmortem agent, Nov 11, 2026, 03:45:50 UTC. Not reviewed yet. Each part is as of when the work it reports ended, which the timeline dates; who ended the incident is as of now.
First told: Argus posted in Slack, Nov 11, 2026, 03:24:34 UTC
Ended by: Argus: reverted the feature flag typical-purchase-feature - confirmed, still in place

Summary
The service broke at 03:18 UTC and was back to normal at 03:25:24 UTC, 7 minutes 24 seconds later. What its alert watches went from 198 ms before it began to 2083 ms at its worst. The shop's takings fell short of the same hours on earlier weeks by no more than those hours vary on their own, if at all. Switching on a feature made the shop use a new way of working out a shopper's typical spend, and that method likely slows down sharply for shoppers with a long purchase history, so their pages took much longer to load. What Argus did: reverted the feature flag typical-purchase-feature (can be put back) - confirmed, still in place. Argus opened a draft fix, PR #545, for a person to review and merge. Switching typical-purchase-feature back on, or sending any other request to the typical-spend calculation, could again make requests for shoppers with long purchase histories very slow.

Impact
7m 24s - onset until back to normal
1.2% to 1.2% - error rate, before onset and while broken on average (no rise)
198 ms to 1406 ms - what the alert watches, before onset and while broken on average (worst minute 2083 ms; the rule's line is 500 ms)
none - customer loss (estimated)

Root cause and contributing factors
With use_typical_spend true, render_spend_summary calls typical_spend_per_item (src/io_shop/typical_spend.py). Code-Fix read that function as finding the middle price by repeatedly scanning the whole purchase history for its minimum and then scanning it again to remove it, many times over. Its work therefore grows far faster than the history's length, so requests for shoppers with long histories pay a large cost. It rests on F1, a reading of the source nothing ran, so it is unverified.
Causal chain
symptom The slowest requests to io-shop took far longer than usual. Its slowest-request latency rose from the minute the incident began, and no more requests failed than before.
  Evidence:
    AL1 p99 latency above threshold for 5m
    T5 03:25:02 Investigator Agent: Placed the start of the incident at 03:18
why 1 Requests started going through the flag-on path when admin switched typical-purchase-feature on at 03:18:23 UTC. Before that, the service's flag evaluations were all off (Ga6f5). They were split during 03:18 UTC (Gc8c4) and all on from then until the alert (Gd44a).
  Evidence:
    P1 03:18:23 UTC flag toggle typical-purchase-feature by admin: feature flag typical-purchase-feature was switched on
    Ga6f5 INFO io-shop: typical-purchase-feature=off - 200 evaluations - 30 occurrences in 30 minutes, 02:48–03:17
    Gc8c4 INFO io-shop: typical-purchase-feature=off 77 / on 123 - 200 evaluations - 1 occurrence in 1 minute, 03:18
    Gd44a INFO io-shop: typical-purchase-feature=on - 200 evaluations - 6 occurrences in 6 minutes, 03:19–03:24
  Ruled out:
    A deploy or release on the service: the Investigator Agent asked for production change events - deploys, releases and flag changes on the service, the 1 day 1 minute before Nov 11 03:19; the Investigator Agent read back 1 production change.
      T7
      T8
    Any other flag change: the flag provider's history showed no flag change by anyone but Argus other than this switch in the period read.
      T14 03:25:08 Argus: Read the flag provider's history - 1 flag change by anyone but Argus, the 1 hour before 03:25:08
why 2 With the flag on, render_spend_summary calls typical_spend_per_item to build the shopper's spend summary.
  Evidence:
    F1 What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed - nothing ran its test or its fix
    U1 typical_spend_per_item at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:67, in render_spend_summary: calls it: return typical_spend_per_item(account)
why 3 Code-Fix read typical_spend_per_item's work as growing far faster than a shopper's purchase history, so requests for shoppers with long histories became slow.
  Evidence:
    F1
Contributing factors
- Before typical-purchase-feature was switched on, no check was seen that measured the latency of the code path it enabled for shoppers with long purchase histories. (AI-3)
- The flag was switched on for all traffic in one step: evaluations went from all off to all on almost immediately, and no gradual rollout was seen. (AI-4)
- No test was seen that bounds how much work typical_spend_per_item does on a long purchase history. (AI-2)

Hypotheses considered
 | Hypothesis | Confidence | Result
C1 | The feature flag typical-purchase-feature was switched from off to on at 03:18:23 UTC. From that minute p99 latency rose from about 200ms to between 750ms and 2083ms. Error rate, p50, p95, memory, CPU and traffic stayed at baseline. No deployment or placement change accompanied it. | 0.88 | confirmed

Trigger
typical-purchase-feature flag went from OFF to ON at 03:18:23 UTC, by admin.

Resolution
 | Time (UTC) | Action | By | Kind | Outcome
M1 | 03:25:24 | Reverted the feature flag typical-purchase-feature for C1 | Argus | can be put back | confirmed, still in place
 | 03:29:52 | Proposed a fix: PR #545 | Code-Fix Agent | nothing to put back | opened as a draft

Detection
The incident on io-shop began at 03:18 UTC. HighLatency fired at 03:24:11 UTC, 6 minutes 11 seconds later.
What the alert said
AL1 | p99 latency above threshold for 5m

Action items
Item | Action | Type | Owner | Tracking | Status
AI-1 | Reverted the feature flag typical-purchase-feature | mitigate | Argus | - | done
AI-2 | Review and merge the proposed fix | prevent | unassigned | PR #545 | open
AI-3 | Before any feature flag that enables a new code path is switched on in production, require a latency check of that path against accounts with long purchase histories. | prevent | unassigned | - | open
AI-4 | Roll out io-shop feature flags to a small share of traffic first, and widen them only while slowest-request latency stays at baseline. | prevent | unassigned | - | open
AI-5 | Link the HighLatency alert on io-shop to an on-call rotation so that it pages a person. | process | unassigned | - | open
AI-6 | Make average_spend_per_item in spend_summary.py scale to long histories, and add a test that bounds its work. This is the flag-off path, which Code-Fix read as also growing far faster than history length. | prevent | unassigned | - | open

Lessons learned
What went well
- The alert came within the 7 minutes 30 seconds accounted for by its rule waiting 5 minutes with its condition holding, its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute the onset is measured to.
- 57 seconds after the alert was raised, the Investigator Agent formed 1 candidate cause, best first: C1.
- 1 minute 13 seconds after the alert was raised, the Mitigation Agent reverted the feature flag typical-purchase-feature for C1, moved from ON to OFF.
- 3 minutes 54 seconds after the alert was raised, the Mitigation Agent judged the action CONFIRMED.
- 5 minutes 41 seconds after the alert was raised, the Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as a draft pull request - PR #545.
What went wrong
- The alert paged nobody: no on-call incident was linked to it.
Where it got lucky
Nothing.

Response effort
none - engineer time
152,688 - tokens spent by Argus

Supporting information
The incident's walk: http://localhost:8000/incidents/08f7336f-92bd-4dc4-a081-2ea733f65ba4
The fix it proposed: PR #545 (https://github.com/ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App/pull/545) opened as a draft. The record holds nothing about it after that.
Changes to production read
P1 | 03:18:23 UTC flag toggle typical-purchase-feature by admin: feature flag typical-purchase-feature was switched on
Deploys read, none came back.
Log messages read (UTC)
Ga6f5 | INFO io-shop: typical-purchase-feature=off - 200 evaluations - 30 occurrences in 30 minutes, 02:48–03:17
G46bc | ERROR io-shop: account page request failed - ClientDisconnected: the shopper closed the connection - 60 occurrences in 37 minutes, 02:48–03:24
Gbac1 | WARN io-shop: account page error rate at #% over the last minute - 34 occurrences in 37 minutes, 02:48–03:24; # was 0.50% to 2.50%, typically 1.00%, highest at 02:59
Gad41 | INFO io-shop: account pages rendered normally - 3 occurrences in 31 minutes, 02:49–03:19
Gc8c4 | INFO io-shop: typical-purchase-feature=off 77 / on 123 - 200 evaluations - 1 occurrence in 1 minute, 03:18
Gd44a | INFO io-shop: typical-purchase-feature=on - 200 evaluations - 6 occurrences in 6 minutes, 03:19–03:24
What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed - nothing ran its test or its fix
F1 | The fault is in src/io_shop/typical_spend.py. typical_spend_per_item is the function render_spend_summary in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py calls when use_typical_spend is true. To find the middle price it ran remaining.remove(min(remaining)) (n-1)//2 times. Each pass scans the whole list for the minimum and then scans it again to remove that element, so the work grows with the square of the history's length. For shoppers with a short history that cost is small. For shoppers with a long history it is large. That fits a p99-only rise from the moment the flag sent requests into this path, with p50 and p95 flat. The flag only exposed it: any request routed here would have paid this cost.

The change: sort the prices once and take index (len - 1) // 2. That is O(n log n) and gives the same answer the loop did: the lower of the two middles on an even-length history, with each repeated price counted once per purchase. For an empty history the old code raised ValueError from min([]). The new code raises ValueError itself, so callers that handle that see the same exception type as before. The function's signature and the caller in spend_summary.py are unchanged.

The test: tests/io_shop/test_typical_spend.py keeps its existing correctness cases and adds two. The first is a bound on work. It builds a shuffled 2000-purchase history from an int subclass that counts < and == comparisons, and asserts the count stays under 4·n·log2(n). The remove-the-minimum loop needs roughly n²/2 comparisons (about two million here) and is written to exceed the bound. A single sort is written to fit well inside it. The second checks that an empty history still raises ValueError.

Not changed: average_spend_per_item in spend_summary.py also re-sums a prefix on every pass, which is quadratic too. That is the long-standing flag-off path, not the one this flag switched on, so I left it alone to keep this diff small. It deserves its own follow-up.
How the code outside Code-Fix's patch uses what it changes, read on main
U1 | typical_spend_per_item at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:67, in render_spend_summary: calls it: return typical_spend_per_item(account)
Assumptions
- Exchange rate: EUR converted at 0.92191 per USD, published 2026-11-10
- No engineer minutes: no on-call incident was linked to this one, so nobody was paged to respond

The document, by field:
overview: For {duration}, the slowest io-shop requests took longer than usual to load. The slowdown began when a feature was switched on that changed how the shop works out a shopper's typical spend. That new method likely slows down for shoppers with a long purchase history, so their pages took longer to load. Argus estimates the cost to the shop in lost takings at {customer_loss}. Nobody was paged, because no on-call incident was linked to this one. Argus reverted the feature flag typical-purchase-feature, and that change is confirmed and still in place. Argus has also proposed a fix, which is open as a draft and has not been applied.

Not to be judged:
  - Names in braces, such as {duration}, are figures code writes in from the list of figures in the ask. They are not judged.
  - The overview is written in plain words for the people who lead the company. A claim said more plainly than the postmortem says it is grounded where it means the same.

Judge every claim in the document, and answer by calling judge_claims.

tools.description: Submit every claim in the document, each either as supported or as flagged. Supported: the document's own words, quoted exactly, and the record's rows that support it. Flagged: the document's own words, quoted exactly, why, and the record's rows that contradict it (none where no row speaks to it at all). Empty lists say the document makes no claim to judge.

why.description: One sentence: what the record holds instead. Never empty.
